# The manifest says what this export is, and what it could not resolve.
.dist/manifest.json :: "formatVersion": 1
.dist/manifest.json :: "target": "none"
.dist/manifest.json :: "humanBase": null
.dist/manifest.json :: "type": "glossary"

# Two counts, named apart: three records, five terms between them. One number would be read as either,
# and the term count is not derivable without opening the flat file.
.dist/manifest.json :: "records": 3
.dist/manifest.json :: "parts": 5
.dist/manifest.json :: "partsFile": "glossary/terms.jsonl"

# A record carries what `export:` in the schema declares, and not what it does not. `owner` stays
# behind: it is a fact about this corpus's stewardship rather than about the words.
.dist/glossary/gls-search.json :: "narrows": "gls-estate"
.dist/glossary/gls-search.json :: "status": "draft"
.dist/glossary/gls-search.json :: "review-by": "2030-01-01"
.dist/glossary/gls-search.json :: !"owner"

# One spelling of absent, in every file and for every key. A root narrows nothing, and says so the way
# a term with no labelled line says it.
.dist/glossary/gls-estate.json :: "narrows": null
.dist/glossary/terms.jsonl :: "not":null

# Prose arrives unwrapped: the corpus's 120-column wrap is a fact about the file, and a grep for a
# phrase straddling it would match nothing. The blank line the author wrote is kept.
.dist/glossary/gls-estate.json :: "Scope": "What every system here has in common. A word only one system uses belongs in that system's glossary, and a word two of them disagree about belongs here with the disagreement named.\n\nA word two systems use
.dist/glossary/terms.jsonl :: "not":"a branch in source control. Both appear in the same sentence often enough to be worth separating, and a reader arriving from either one will read the other as a mistake."

# A corpus with no resolvable address writes its records without links rather than with empty ones.
.dist/glossary/gls-search.json :: "links": null

# One term, one line, one whole object — carrying the definition and the labelled line apart, the state
# of the glossary it came from, and the record it belongs to, because a grep hands back a line and
# nothing around it.
.dist/glossary/terms.jsonl :: {"id":"gls-search.query","title":"Query","definition":"What a reader typed, after parsing and before matching.","not":"the request the service received. One request carries a query and its paging.","seeAlso":null,"type":"glossary","record":"gls-search","part":"query","status":"draft","reviewBy":"2030-01-01","links":null}

# A cross-reference travels as a part id the consumer can look up. The source names the file and not
# the anchor, so the counterpart is this term's own id inside the record pointed at — and the prose
# keeps the reference its author wrote.
.dist/glossary/terms.jsonl :: "seeAlso":["gls-framework.record"]
.dist/glossary/terms.jsonl :: "not":"a knowledge document filed under a type — see [gls-framework]."

# Generality holds inside a chain: `gls-search` narrows `gls-estate`, so a grep for a term both define
# would meet the general one first. Across `gls-estate` and `gls-framework` — unrelated roots, both
# defining `record` — the order is stable and claims nothing, so nothing here asserts it does.
.dist/glossary/terms.jsonl :: "record":"gls-estate","part":"record"
.dist/glossary/terms.jsonl :: "record":"gls-framework","part":"record"
